title: Health Status and Treatment Plan: A Physical Examination Report for Higher Education in Different Countries

context_sources.name: Dooris, Cawood, Doherty and Powell, Healthy universities, 2010
Waas et al., Sustainable higher education, 2012
World Bank World Development Indicators and Education Statistics
Liu and Wang, DEA Malmquist productivity measure, 2008

limitations: Running headers and a watermark leak into every page and scramble several tables.
The AHP comparison matrix is legible only in pieces; the weights and CR are printed in prose.
Table 1's rows are misaligned by the OCR, so indicator symbols were checked against the prose.
The Markov threshold is printed as 0.05 on both sides, which leaves the middle state empty.

tasks: Build a health measure for a national higher education system and grade it
Apply both to several countries and choose one with room to improve
Set a vision and targeted policies with a timeline

section_map.summary: Point-gain health score, Malmquist sustainability, five countries, India treated in three phases.
A model alone is not enough; policy must match the country's conditions.
Six assumptions, built on a medical analogy, including a population that does not exist.
Six factors, fourteen indicators, fifty countries, three impact codes.
AHP weights, quantile health ranges, six grades, then DEA-Malmquist with a decline rule.
US, UK, Germany, Japan, India diagnosed on both models.
Three-phase vision, six policies, a Markov forecast, four real-world obstacles.
Four strengths, two weaknesses, both about the health range.

contributions.summary: Health as a weighted count of passes against a reference range, so each failure stays traceable.
Sustainability reduced to a count of consecutive efficiency declines.
Policy speed treated as random, with the push weakening as the indicator nears its bound.

dependency_graph.handoff: The same fourteen indicators are split into inputs and outputs for the efficiency model
The health ranges are the normal values the chain pushes each indicator toward

assumptions.summary: The chosen indicators share the distribution of a population that the authors say does not exist.
Every indicator has one interval that separates healthy from not.
Next year's policy effect depends only on this year's state and on the gap from normal.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Fifty countries, 2009 to 2018. Sources named per indicator: World Bank, Wikipedia, QS, Web of Science, Nature Index.

models.summary: AHP weights and a zero-one score against quantile and normal ranges.
CCR efficiency extended by Malmquist ratios, graded by consecutive declines.
A three-state Markov update pushing indicators toward their healthy bounds.

verification.summary: K-S test at 0.05 plus Q-Q plots for GPI and employment.

results_trace.summary: US point sequence ends in a single zero, score 0.964, sub-healthy, efficiency rising.
UK score 0.964, employment slightly over its cap, sustainability poor.
Japan score 0.7774, unhealthy from investment and gender equity, but sustainable.
India score 0.5783, extremely unhealthy, efficiency down four years running.
Twenty runs: employment about 10 years, enrollment about 13, net flow about 48. Timeline 2018, 2028, 2031, 2066, 2118.

writing_logic.summary: The introduction says a model is not enough and poses the policy question before any model appears.
An indicator is dropped with a reason, and another is rejected after being tried.
Each recommended policy is followed by the harm it can do.

language_observations.summary: Five verdicts are delivered in one sentence, each country with both a health grade and a sustainability grade.
The population behind the distribution is admitted not to exist, in the same breath as the assumption.
The rule counts consecutive declines and then explains each count in ordinary words.
The long-run cause and the immediate need are stated together, and the second wins.
The hardest obstacle is a social fact the law has already abolished.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: map of the fifty selected countries.
Figure 2: the examination workflow, from data to both diagnoses.
Figure 3: the AHP steps, with the consistency test as a branch.
Figures 5 and 6: K-S results for GPI and employment.
Figures 7 and 8: Q-Q plots for the same two indicators.
Figure 9: the score thresholds for the six grades.
Figures 11 and 12: efficiency paths for the US and the UK.
Figures 13 and 14: efficiency paths for Germany and Japan.

Figure 18: predicted net flow of international students.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A pass-fail score keeps every failed indicator visible, which a blended index hides.
A sustainability rule a reader can apply by counting is worth more than a trend described in adjectives.
Naming the harm of one's own policy, including a wage cut that hurts the poor, reads as judgment rather than advocacy.

weaknesses.summary: The 80 percent healthy share is fixed from QS rankings, not estimated.
The Markov parameters are chosen, and the printed threshold leaves no middle state.
Authors: too few countries for the fitted range, and the 2018 bounds are held fixed for a century.

independent_extensions.summary: Let the health bounds move with the sample instead of freezing them at 2018.
Estimate the step size and the state thresholds instead of setting them.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Grade against a reference range per indicator, with the bound direction set by the indicator's type.
Policy split into horizons, each aimed at a stated score and a stated year.

unresolved_questions.question: What value of k is used for each indicator, and where does the middle state sit if both thresholds are 0.05?
Why three consecutive declines and not two or four?
